latin_text: iam Cherubico spiritu animati, per scalarum idest naturae gradus philosophantes, a centro ad centrum omnia pervadentes, nunc unum quasi Osyrim in multitudinem vi Titanica discerpentes descendemus, nunc multitudinem quasi Osyridis membra in unum vi Phebea colligentes ascendemus, donec, in sinu Patris – qui super scalas est – tandem quiescentes, theologica foelicitate consumabimur.
english_translation: Once we, inspired by the cherubic spirit, have reached this point through the art of speaking or of reasoning – that is, philosophizing according to the grades of Nature, penetrating the whole from the centre to the centre – then shall we descend, dashing the one into many with Titanic force like Osiris, and ascend, drawing together with Phoebean might the many into one, like Osiris's limbs, until at last, resting in the bosom of the Father Who is at the top of the ladder, we shall be made perfect in theological bliss.
exegesis:
[VERIFIED] This passage describes the actual philosophical practice through which humans become angelified. Inspired by the *Cherubico spiritu* (Cherubic spirit), the practitioner philosophizes *per scalarum idest naturae gradus*—along the rungs of the ladder, which is nature itself. The phrase *a centro ad centrum* (*from center to center, penetrating all things*) suggests that the practitioner moves from the center of their own soul through all intermediate realities to the center of cosmic order and thence to God. Then the practice oscillates between two complementary operations: (*descendemus*) the analytical descent—*dashing the one into many with Titanic force* (like Osiris scattered into fragments by the Titans)—and (*ascendemus*) the synthetic ascent—*gathering the many into one with Phoebean might* (like the god Osiris reconstituted and made whole by Isis).

The philosophical function is to describe the actual contemplative method that achieves angelic transformation. Analysis (the Titanic operation) breaks down the apparent multiplicity of phenomena into their underlying archai—first principles. The practitioner descends through creation, examining each level's relationship to its causes, tracing multiplicity back to unity. Synthesis (the Phoebean operation, named for Apollo/Phoebus, god of harmony and wholeness) reverses this, ascending from principles to particulars, gathering the fragmentary into coherent wholes. This alternation between analysis and synthesis—between breaking apart and reintegrating—corresponds to the angelic activity of ascent and descent. The cherubic spirit, which already possesses this integrative wisdom, animates the practitioner's effort.

The passage culminates in henosis: *donec, in sinu Patris – qui super scalas est – tandem quiescentes, theologica foelicitate consumabimur* (until at last, resting in the bosom of the Father Who is at the top of the ladder, we are fulfilled in theological bliss). The ladder, the ascending-descending, the analysis-synthesis, all terminate in rest (*quiescentes*) at the Source. The achieved state is *theologica foelicitas*—theological happiness or beatitude—the perfection (*consumabimur*, from *consummare*, to fulfill completely) toward which all philosophy aims. [INFERRED] Heptaplus 7.7 (the seventh day/rest) parallels this culmination in divine rest. The Commento Book IV describes this as the consummation of all mystical theology. Being & Unity grounds this metaphysically in the final actualization of participated being—the creature perfectly receiving and resting in the divine actuality.
notes: The practitioner becomes inspired by the cherubic spirit and ascends/descends the ladder of nature, ultimately resting in the Father's bosom. This is the mystical goal: perfection in 'theological bliss' (perfectio/henosis).
